summary: Describes how Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) are assigned to past and future RFCs. A DOI is a widely used identifier system that gives documents unique names that can be looked up and managed consistently.

eli5.summary: Every library book gets a permanent code, and this note says how RFCs get theirs.

questions: how are dois assigned to rfcs
what is a digital object identifier
subtitle: Persistent identifiers for RFCs in scholarly publishing

tldr.problem: RFCs are authoritative technical documents, but web URLs can change or disappear. Scholarly publishers need persistent, unique identifiers for documents to ensure stable citations and easy discovery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Editor registers all RFCs with CrossRef, a registration agency for Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). Each RFC gets a DOI following the pattern 10.17487/rfcN (where N is the RFC number), which maps to the RFC Editor's info page and provides bibliographic metadata.
tldr.outcome: RFCs can now be cited with DOIs in scholarly publications, enabling automatic bibliographic lookup and linking through systems like BibTeX. The RFC Editor maintains a DOI for every RFC published, past and future.

today: RFC 7669 is an informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. The RFC Editor continues to assign DOIs to all published RFCs. All RFCs published since this document have DOIs, and DOIs are included in RFC metadata available to publishers, libraries, and citation systems.

sections.title: What Are DOIs and Why RFCs Need Them
sections.content:
A Digital Object Identifier (DOI) is a persistent, unique identifier for digital content that is managed by the International DOI Foundation. Unlike a web URL, which can change when a website reorganizes, a DOI redirects to the current location of a document through a centralized resolver. Publishers and scholars use DOIs to ensure citations remain valid even when content moves.

The RFC Editor publishes technical specifications used worldwide by internet engineers. RFCs are immutable—a published RFC never changes—making them ideal candidates for persistent identifiers. By assigning DOIs, the RFC Editor makes it easier for RFCs to be cited in scholarly databases, journal articles, and technical references. The DOI also carries bibliographic metadata (author, title, publication date) that libraries and indexing services can query.
sections.eli5: DOIs are like permanent reference numbers. When you use an RFC's DOI, it automatically finds the RFC even if the RFC Editor's website reorganizes.

sections.title: How DOIs Work for RFCs
sections.content:
The RFC Editor chose CrossRef as its DOI registration agency. CrossRef is widely used by journal publishers and charges membership and per-document fees. The RFC Editor's DOI prefix is 10.17487. The DOI suffix for an RFC is based on the RFC number (without zero-padding), so RFC 1149 has the DOI 10.17487/rfc1149.

When someone looks up this DOI at the resolver https://dx.doi.org/, it redirects to the RFC Editor's info page (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc1149), which has the document abstract, links to different formats (text, PDF, HTML), and metadata. The RFC Editor retroactively assigned DOIs to all previously published RFCs by updating its internal database and submitting metadata to CrossRef. New RFCs receive DOIs automatically at publication time.

RFC authors and indexing services can include DOIs in reference sections. Standards like xml2rfc (the XML markup for RFCs) support DOIs in the seriesInfo field, so bibliography tools can retrieve and format them automatically.
sections.eli5: Every RFC gets a permanent code like 10.17487/rfc1149. When you type that code into a DOI resolver, it finds the RFC no matter where it lives online.

sections.title: Scholarly and Practical Benefits
sections.content:
DOIs enable RFCs to be indexed and cited like traditional scholarly publications. Academic databases can include RFCs with full bibliographic information. BibTeX and other citation managers can fetch RFC metadata from DOI resolvers automatically. Libraries and research tools like the ACM Digital Library benefit from having DOIs in RFC references, as DOIs link directly to the RFC Editor rather than to paywalled copies elsewhere.

The DOI system adds no dependency on the RFC Editor itself for availability—if the RFC Editor's website went down, DOI resolvers would still resolve to the authoritative location. The RFC text remains immutable and unchanged by the DOI system, so this is purely an addition to how RFCs are discovered and cited. The RFC Style Guide was updated to document the rules for including DOIs in RFC reference sections.
sections.eli5: Using DOIs makes RFCs appear in library and academic citation systems the same way journal articles do, so they are easier to find and cite formally.

sections.title: Integration into Scholarly Systems
sections.content: Assigning DOIs to RFCs integrates them into the scholarly publishing ecosystem. This makes RFCs discoverable in academic databases and citable in formal publications like journal articles. The RFC Editor implemented this by registering with CrossRef and submitting metadata for all RFCs past and future. The process is transparent to readers and authors but enables better access and proper academic attribution for the RFC series. Future RFCs automatically receive DOIs at publication time, ensuring the practice continues indefinitely.
sections.eli5: DOIs turn RFCs into proper scholarly documents that libraries and academic systems recognize, so scientists can cite them like any research paper.
